implementation_notes: Boost.Pool's object_pool<T> is the classic C++ realisation: chunks are allocated in blocks and recycled through the pool's free list, while construct()/destroy() run the element's constructor and destructor so typed objects can be created and returned to the pool (std::pmr pool resources pool memory blocks from C++17, std::hive<T> reuses erased element slots from C++26). Choose an ordered pool when you frequently allocate arrays (frees stay O(N) otherwise), keep Object Usage - one pool per thread - unless you need the synchronised Singleton Usage interfaces, and remember what none of these facilities does: clear application state that lives outside the constructor. The library owns storage reuse; reset remains yours.
pitfalls: object_pool re-runs the constructor via construct() but knows nothing about application-level reset: state initialised outside the constructor must be cleared by the caller.
Element types must have a non-throwing destructor, and Object Usage pools are not thread-safe - one pool per thread, or use the Singleton Usage interfaces, which synchronise their access.
Unordered free lists make single-object malloc/free O(1) but can miss free capacity on array requests; ordered pools fix that at the cost of O(N) frees.

variants.name: std::pmr pool resources (C++17)
variants.implementation_notes: C++17's <memory_resource> ships pooling as a standard library type: a pool resource owns chunks split into equal-size blocks and serves each request from the pool fitting the requested size, geometrically growing chunks when a pool runs dry. Pair it with polymorphic_allocator so containers and objects allocate from the pool; use synchronized_pool_resource when several threads share it and unsynchronized_pool_resource when a single thread owns it (cheaper, and it may keep thread-specific pools). It pools memory blocks, not application state, so reset semantics remain yours.
pitfalls: The resource must outlive every object allocated from it; destroying it first leaves dangling allocations, and release() is the only way to reclaim memory early.
Requests above the largest block size are served from the upstream allocator, so huge objects silently bypass pooling.
Mixing allocators from different resources for one container is undefined; a container and its elements must share the resource.

variants.name: std::hive<T> container (C++26)
variants.implementation_notes: C++26 adds std::hive<T>, a sequence container whose insertion position is unspecified precisely so it can reuse the memory locations of erased elements while keeping pointers and iterators to live elements valid. For workloads that pool objects to avoid allocation and fragmentation, this removes the hand-written free list entirely: erase() returns the slot to the container and later insertion reuses it. It is a container, not a lease API - there is no checkout/borrow contract - so pending state reset and capacity limits (reserve/trim_capacity/block limits) remain application responsibilities.
pitfalls: Insertion position is unspecified and iteration order is unstable, so it fits pools better than ordered collections.
There is no borrow/return contract: nothing prevents concurrent use of an 'erased then re-inserted' element, and per-element reset is still yours.
It is C++26-only (feature-test macro __cpp_lib_hive); earlier toolchains need plf::colony or Boost.Pool to get the same behaviour.
